answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**Defendant Must Show That There Is No Reasonable Basis to Predict That Plaintiff Might Recover Against the In-State Defendant.**

A party that removes on diversity grounds despite the presence of an in-state defendant must prove that the defendant was improperly joined. The burden belongs entirely to the remover, and it is a heavy one. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 574 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc); *accord Flagg v. Stryker Corp.*, 819 F.3d 132, 136 (5th Cir. 2016) (en banc); *Mumfrey v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc.*, 719 F.3d 392, 401 (5th Cir. 2013). Plaintiff need not prove that joinder was proper. Defendant must prove that it was not.

**A. The governing test asks whether there is any reasonable basis for recovery.**

Improper joinder may be established in only two ways: "(1) actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts, or (2) inability of the plaintiff to establish a cause of action against the non-diverse party in state court." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573 (quoting *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 646–47 (5th Cir. 2003)). Under the second, the question is "whether the defendant has demonstrated that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Id.*; *see also Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011).

The standard requires a reasonable possibility of recovery; a merely theoretical one will not suffice. *Great Plains Tr. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co.*, 313 F.3d 305, 312 (5th Cir. 2002). But Plaintiff need not show that he will, or probably will, prevail. *See Guillory v. PPG Indus., Inc.*, 434 F.3d 303, 308–09 (5th Cir. 2005). Doubt about the outcome does not carry Defendant's burden.

**B. Contested facts and unsettled law are resolved for Plaintiff.**

In deciding whether Defendant has made the required showing, the Court resolves contested factual issues and ambiguities in controlling state law in Plaintiff's favor. *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649; *see McKee v. Kan. City S. Ry. Co.*, 358 F.3d 329, 333–34 (5th Cir. 2004). A removing defendant therefore cannot prevail by offering a competing account of disputed events or by urging the more favorable reading of an unsettled point of state law. The jurisdictional inquiry is not an occasion to try the merits.

**C. The Court's limited procedure does not shift or dilute the burden.**

The Court ordinarily begins with a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis of the allegations against the in-state defendant. If those allegations survive that analysis, there ordinarily is no improper joinder. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. The federal pleading standard governs this review. *Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 200 (5th Cir. 2016).

Where a complaint states a claim but has misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine the propriety of joinder, the Court has discretion to pierce the pleadings and conduct a summary inquiry. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. That inquiry is narrow. It exists to identify discrete and undisputed facts that would preclude recovery, not to permit substantial discovery or a pretrial resolution of the merits. *Id.* at 573–74. Nor may Defendant establish improper joinder through a defense that equally disposes of the claims against the diverse defendant; such a showing attacks the merits of the case as a whole, not the joinder of the in-state party. *Id.* at 574–76.

Accordingly, Defendant must demonstrate that no reasonable basis exists to predict that Plaintiff might recover against **[In-State Defendant]**. Unless it does so, complete diversity is lacking, the Court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, and the case must be remanded. *See* 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c).
